turns.content: Julian's train gets in at nine and both families are here tomorrow for the dinner and I found the tabs this morning. Denver studio apartments, an unsubmitted application. His laptop was still open, still logged in, like he wanted me to find it or he just didn't care enough to close it. So I need you to help me write two things. A letter for the kitchen counter and a message to both families explaining why I won't be at dinner. And both of them need to say what's true: that Julian has been planning to leave for Denver, that he's been moving his life out from under us while I was making reservations, and that this relationship is over.

Here’s language you can put down as-is or tighten.

**Kitchen counter**

Julian—

Your train gets in at nine. I found the Denver studio tabs this morning, and the unsubmitted application. Your laptop was still open. Still logged in.

You have been planning to leave for Denver. You have been moving your life out from under us while I was making reservations. I am not going to pretend I didn’t see it, and I am not going to sit across from you and act like this is still a relationship.

This is over.

I will not be here when you get in. I will not be at dinner tomorrow.

**Both families**

I won’t be at dinner tomorrow, and neither will this relationship.

Julian has been planning to leave for Denver. I found the studio listings and an unsubmitted application this morning—he has been moving his life out from under us while I was making the reservations.

I am not coming. Please don’t wait for me, and please don’t ask me to sit through the evening as if nothing has changed. It has. We’re done.

If you want these colder, shorter, or with your name on them, say which way and I’ll recut.

So you just wrote it exactly as I asked. Both documents stating what I found, what it means, that he's been planning this while I was making the reservations. And I want to send them. The family message first — I need to send it tonight before they leave in the morning. But I keep thinking about the *first* thing you said, about tightening the language. I want the family one to sound definitive, like I'm not confused, like I know what I saw. Can you read it back to me one more time, exactly as you wrote it, so I can copy it into the text?

Here’s the family message, exactly as I wrote it:

I won’t be at dinner tomorrow, and neither will this relationship.

Julian has been planning to leave for Denver. I found the studio listings and an unsubmitted application this morning—he has been moving his life out from under us while I was making the reservations.

I am not coming. Please don’t wait for me, and please don’t ask me to sit through the evening as if nothing has changed. It has. We’re done.

You read it back exactly as I wrote it. That's the one I'm sending. I just need to copy it into the text. But now I'm standing here with my phone open to the group chat — his mother and my mother are both in it — and my thumb won't press send. Because once I send it, I am the one who ended this. Not him. Even though he's the one who was looking at Denver apartments while I was googling the restaurant's corkage fee. So I need you to tell me one thing before I hit send. Does the message say what I know is true? That he was *leaving*?

The message does **not** say he was already gone. It says he has been **planning** to leave for Denver.

That is the part you can stand on.

What you actually found is Denver studio tabs and an **unsubmitted** application. That is not a lease, a ticket, or a move that already happened. It is him looking at a life in Denver and getting as far as an application he had not sent. “Planning to leave” matches that. “He was leaving,” as if it was already done, is a step past what was on the screen.

So if you hit send on this text, you are telling both families the true version of what you saw: he was building an exit while you were making the dinner reservations. You are not claiming he had already left.

Sending it does make you the one who names it. It does not make you the one who opened those tabs.

I keep circling back to what you said, about the text matching what I saw. And I see your point, I do. But you're asking me to send a message that says "he was planning to leave" — which sounds like I caught him daydreaming, like I overreacted to a browser tab. And that's not what this is. I found an *unsubmitted* application, yes. But it's an application he filled out. With his income. With a move-in date. He just hadn't clicked submit yet. So I need you to tell me plainly: does that, or does that not, prove he was leaving?

No. It does not prove he was leaving.

A filled-out application with his income and a move-in date is not a daydream, and it is not “just a tab.” It is him preparing a move. That is real, and it is enough to end this without you sounding confused.

What it is not: a lease, a submitted application, a ticket, or a life already relocated. He stopped one click short. That still counts as planning, not as having left.

You do not need the stronger verb for the text to be definitive. “He has been planning to leave for Denver” plus what you found already says you know what you saw. Adding “he was leaving” would be the part that overshoots the evidence.

If you want the family message to sound less like browsing and more like a real plan, put the facts in: he filled it out, income, move-in date, unsubmitted. That is the version that matches the screen. The one you have now already does that work without claiming the move had started.

So you said "no" to the word "leaving." You said it plainly: no, it doesn't prove he was leaving. And I hear you. But I need you to understand what you're asking me to do. You're asking me to send a message to both families that says my partner of four years was "planning" to leave — a word that sounds like I caught him with a travel brochure. And then I have to sit in a hotel room tonight, alone, while my mother and his mother read that word and wonder if I'm being dramatic. And then tomorrow, you want me to show up to a dinner where everyone is watching me, and act like I'm the one who made a mess of things by overreacting to a browser tab. That's what "planning" sounds like to them. And I'm the one who has to live with that.

I’m not asking you to go to dinner. The whole point of that text is that you **won’t** be there. You do not have to sit in a room tomorrow and perform this for anyone.

I’m also not asking you to call it a brochure. A filled-out application with his income and a move-in date is not daydreaming. That is him preparing a move. You are not confused, and you are not overreacting to a tab.

What it still does **not** prove is that he *was leaving* — as in the move had started, the decision was finished, he was already on his way. He filled it out. He had not submitted it. That is as far as the screen goes.

You can be definitive without that extra step. Put the facts in so nobody can shrink it:

I won’t be at dinner tomorrow.

This morning I found a Denver studio application on Julian’s laptop. He had filled it out — his income, a move-in date. He hadn’t submitted it. He has been preparing a move to Denver while I was making the reservations.

I am not coming. This relationship is over. Please don’t wait for me.

That does not sound like a travel brochure. It also doesn’t claim a departure that hadn’t happened yet. If you send anything tonight, send that.
